content: A contraceptive patch is a transdermal device applied to the skin that releases synthetic hormones, specifically estrogen and progestin, to prevent pregnancy. Its effectiveness is considered comparable to that of the combined oral contraceptive pill. Currently, the only available contraceptive patches are Ortho Evra, marketed in the United States by Ortho-McNeil, and Evra, marketed in Canada by Janssen-Ortho and in the United Kingdom and other countries by Janssen-Cilag. These patches are sold in boxes containing three patches and are available only by prescription. Informally, the contraceptive patch is often referred to as the Patch. To use the contraceptive patch, a woman applies the first patch to one of four approved areas of the body: the upper outer arm, buttocks, abdomen, or thigh. This application can occur either on the first day of her menstrual cycle (day 1) or on the first Sunday following that day, depending on her preference. The day of application is then designated as patch change day. Seven days later, on the next patch change day, the woman removes the old patch and applies a new one to one of the approved locations. This process is repeated weekly for three consecutive weeks. On the fourth patch change day, the patch is removed, and no patch is applied for the following seven days. After this patch-free week, a new patch is applied on the next patch change day, and the cycle begins again. If a woman starts using the patch on day 1 of her menstrual cycle, it becomes effective immediately, and no backup contraception is required. Similarly, if the patch is applied immediately following a first-trimester abortion or miscarriage, it is effective right away, and no additional contraception is needed. However, if the patch is started on the first Sunday after day 1 of the menstrual cycle, backup contraception, such as condoms or spermicide, is necessary for the first seven days of patch use. The contraceptive patch works primarily by preventing ovulation, similar to other combined hormonal contraceptives. It also alters cervical mucus, making it more difficult for sperm to penetrate, and has effects on the endometrium that could theoretically inhibit implantation, although there is no scientific evidence to suggest that implantation is actually prevented. The Ortho Evra patch contains 750 µg of ethinyl estradiol (a synthetic estrogen) and 6000 µg of norelgestromin (a synthetic progestin), while the Evra patch contains 600 µg of ethinyl estradiol and 6000 µg of norelgestromin. Both patches are designed to release approximately 20 µg of ethinyl estradiol and 150 µg of norelgestromin into the bloodstream daily. The effectiveness of the contraceptive patch may be reduced when used concurrently with certain medications, including some antibiotics, antifungals, anticonvulsants, and other drugs that increase the metabolism of contraceptive steroids. However, a pharmacokinetic study demonstrated that the use of tetracycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, does not reduce the effectiveness of the Ortho Evra patch. This finding is particularly relevant when tetracycline-derived antibiotics are prescribed after an abortion to prevent infection. Additionally, drugs containing St. John's Wort are known to interfere with the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. In clinical trials involving 3,330 women who used the Ortho Evra/Evra patch for up to one year, 12% of participants discontinued use due to adverse events. The most common reasons for discontinuation included nausea and/or vomiting (2.4%), application site reactions (1.9%), breast discomfort or pain (1.9%), headache (1.1%), and emotional lability (1.0%). Other frequently reported side effects included breast discomfort or pain (22%), headache (21%), application site reactions (17%), nausea (17%), upper respiratory tract infections (10%), menstrual cramps (10%), and abdominal pain (9%). Breakthrough bleeding or spotting was reported by 18% of users during the first cycle, decreasing to 12% by the third cycle and 8% by the sixth and thirteenth cycles. More severe breakthrough bleeding, requiring more than one pad or tampon per day, was reported by 4% of users in the first cycle, 3% in the third and sixth cycles, and 1% in the thirteenth cycle. All combined hormonal contraceptives, including the contraceptive patch, carry a small but increased risk of thromboembolic events, which can be serious or even fatal. Research into the thromboembolic risks of the Ortho Evra patch compared to combined oral contraceptive pills has yielded conflicting results. One study suggested that patch users may have a twofold increased risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolic events compared to users of oral contraceptives containing 35 µg of estrogen and norgestimate. However, another study concluded that the risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolism for patch users is similar to that of oral contraceptive users. The discrepancy between these findings is difficult to resolve due to overlapping confidence intervals. Additionally, the Associated Press reported in 2004 that fatal adverse events were reported to the FDA at three times the rate for Ortho Evra users compared to oral contraceptive users, although these reports are not based on systematic scientific studies. The risk of cardiovascular events, including thromboembolism, is significantly increased in women over the age of 35 who smoke. As a result, the Ortho Evra package insert strongly advises women who use hormonal contraceptives to avoid smoking. The manufacturer has noted that the patch delivers 60% higher levels of estrogen into the bloodstream compared to oral contraceptives containing 35 µg of estrogen, although the clinical significance of this difference remains unclear. The contraceptive patch has been linked to cases of stroke and thrombosis, and its mechanism of hormone absorption differs from that of oral contraceptives. Several lawsuits have been filed in connection with these risks. For example, a lawsuit filed in 2005 alleged that the manufacturer promoted the patch despite being aware of its health risks and failed to adequately warn users. In another case, documents revealed that nearly 500 adverse event reports were submitted to the FDA for Ortho Evra between 2002 and 2004, compared to only 61 reports for all types of birth control pills during the same period. One lawsuit involved a 14-year-old girl who allegedly died from a blood clot caused by the patch, and her parents have sued the manufacturer, Johnson & Johnson.
